summary: The average Indian holds a mutual fund for about three and a half years. Compounding does not really show up until year nine or ten. Almost all the wealth that quietly goes missing sits in that gap. In part two, Roopa Venkatkrishnan goes through why your fixed deposit carries an interest-rate risk nobody mentions when they sell it to you, why you would never dump gold on a bad week but will dump equity without blinking, why retirement has to be funded first because it is the one goal no bank will lend for, and why chasing the top-ranked fund costs you your beta long before it gets you any alpha.

seo.title: Don’t Exit Equity Too Early: Retirement, SIP & Mutual Fund Lessons
seo.description: Why the average Indian's 3.5-year holding period costs them compounding, the hidden risk in your FD, and why retirement gets funded first.

takeaways.text: The average Indian holds a mutual fund for about three and a half years, and compounding does not show up until year nine or ten. The gap between those two numbers is where most of the wealth goes.
A fixed deposit is not the risk-free thing it is sold as. It carries an interest-rate risk that rarely comes up at the counter.
You would not sell gold or property because of one bad week, but equity gets sold on a dip. The asset did not change, the holding period did.
Retirement is the only goal no bank will fund. Every other goal has a loan behind it, which is why this one gets saved for first.
Chasing the top-ranked fund costs you your beta before it ever gets you alpha, and today's number one will not be number one in six months.
